title: Disinformation in the 2018 brazilian presidential election: An analysis of whatsapp family groups
screen_reason: Quantitative content analysis of 472 political posts actually shared inside ten Brazilian WhatsApp family groups (190 participants) during October 2018, the month of the presidential election. Every post was verified for veracity against the checklist of G1's 'Fato ou Fake' fact-checking project and classified completely true / partially false / totally false, and the paper reports that 60% of the shared posts carried wholly or partially false information (183 false = 38.8%, 100 partially false = 21.2%, 167 true = 35.4%, 22 undetermined = 4.6%). That is a share of shared items carrying misinformation from observed platform data, i.e. SHARING, so the paper is eligible.

estimates.misinfo_def: The paper adopts Volkoff's second disinformation strategy, "información incompleta, tendenciosa o simplemente falsa" [EN: incomplete, biased or simply false information], subdivided into Wardle's (2017) seven types on an increasing scale of intent to deceive - satire/parody, false connection, misleading content, false context, impostor content, manipulated content, fabricated content - and states its focus is the highest levels: "Es este tipo de información intencionadamente falsa, sobre todo en los últimos niveles –contenido manipulado y contenido fabricado– que analizamos" [EN: It is this kind of intentionally false information, above all at the last levels - manipulated content and fabricated content - that we analyse]

estimates.page_loc: English Abstract, p. 2 (the source_quote); the Spanish Results text and Tabla 4 are on p. 6, and the Resumen on p. 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The authors verified each post themselves, applying the checklist from the manual of G1's Brazilian fact-checking project 'Fato ou Fake': whether the headline was sensational, the story unusual or the topic exaggerated; whether the information was ambiguous; the publication date (recirculated content); the authenticity of images and audio; whether a professional news outlet published it; and the information's sources. No coder count, no double-coding and no inter-rater reliability statistic are reported. Note this is a fact-checker's METHOD applied by the researchers, not fact-checkers' verdicts, hence ground_truth = researcher_coding.
estimates.moderator_quote: Tras recibir y organizar los datos de cada grupo, se seleccionaron los contenidos multimedia –texto, imagen fija, vídeo, enlace, pdf y audio– compartidos que correspondían a temas políticos, obteniendo una muestra con 472 publicaciones. Éstas fueron verificadas para identificar si se trataba de una información: 1) completamente verdadera; 2) parcialmente falsa, o 3) totalmente falsa. [EN: After receiving and organising each group's data, the shared multimedia contents - text, still image, video, link, pdf and audio - corresponding to political topics were selected, giving a sample of 472 publications. These were verified to identify whether the information was 1) completely true, 2) partially false, or 3) totally false.]
estimates.notes: The 60% is stated verbatim in the Resumen, the English Abstract, the Results and a pull-quote, so it is not a cross-category sum I computed; it also reconciles exactly with Tabla 4 (183 + 100 = 283 of 472 = 59.96%). SHARING rather than CONTENT because the denominator is posts that group members actually shared, not a corpus of content that exists. QUOTE NOTE: the source_quote is the paper's own English Abstract, which states the figure in one contiguous span; the Spanish Results sentence is broken by the interleaved Tabla 3 in this rendering and reads 'Respecto a la veracidad de la información de los contenidos políticos / compartidos en los grupos familiares, los resultados señalan que un / 60% corresponde a información parcial o completamente falsa (tabla 4).' [EN: As to the veracity of the information in the political content shared in the family groups, the results indicate that 60% corresponds to partially or completely false information (Table 4).] Note the denominator is political posts only: group 7 contributed 0 political posts, so 9 of the 10 groups are effectively represented, and the per-group falsity breakdown promised in the method ('Porcentaje de posts con desinformación recibidos en cada grupo familiar') is never reported.

estimates.notes: Strict-definition variant of the 60% row in the same country x platform x measure cell: it isolates wholly false posts (183/472 = 38.8%) from the partially false ones, so the review can see what the broad/narrow definition choice is worth here - 38.8% versus 60%, a 21-point gap driven entirely by the 'partially false' category. Both values are printed with their counts in Tabla 4. [EN of the source_quote: Posts classified as 'false information' (38.8%) outnumbered those containing true information (35.4%).] A pull-quote on p. 7 restates it as 'Las publicaciones clasificadas como fake news (38,8%) superaron la cifra de las que contenían información verdadera (35,4%)'.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons: (a) 'un 90% de los grupos compartio contenidos sobre los candidatos y sus respectivos partidos politicos' [EN: 90% of the groups shared content about the candidates and their political parties] - a share of groups that discussed politics at all (9 of 10; group 7 posted none), not a share of misinformation, so it is not an actor-level SHARING estimate of misinformation either. (b) Format composition (Tabla 3: still image 229 = 48.5%, video 154 = 32.6%, link 41 = 8.7%, text 33 = 7.0%, audio 14 = 3.0%, pdf 1 = 0.2%) - content formats, not veracity. (c) 'Verdadera 167 (35,4%)' - the converse of the construct; and 'Otros 22 (4,6%)', posts whose veracity and provenance could not be determined, which I left out of every numerator. (d) 'Parcialmente falsa 100 (21,2%)' as a standalone row - it is a middle category rather than a nested definition; it is already inside the 60% row and its complement to the 38.8% row, and both counts are recorded in value_raw. (e) Per-group falsity percentages - promised as objective 2 of the method but never reported; Tabla 2 gives only posts per group (54, 14, 50, 115, 41, 79, 0, 40, 47, 32 = 472), so no group-level sub-rows are possible without inventing them. (f) Figures cited from other work and excluded per R8: '62% de los adultos estadounidenses se informara a traves de las redes sociales' (Gottfried & Shearer 2016) and 'el publico declara creer en informacion falsa en un 75% de las ocasiones' (Silverman & Singer-Vine 2016). (g) The 14 groups originally donated, 4 discarded for incomplete data, and the 22 people who declined to participate (having left their family group over election arguments or deleted its content) - recruitment figures; note they imply selection on the very behaviour being measured, which is a real risk-of-bias point rather than an estimate.

rob.design: Cross-sectional web content analysis of donated private WhatsApp data - a design almost unobtainable at the time, and correspondingly non-probabilistic. Recruitment: an open call posted in Facebook and WhatsApp groups for 15 days, with an anonymity guarantee; 14 family groups were donated and 4 discarded for incomplete data, leaving 10 groups (190 participants) from Sao Paulo, Rio Grande do Sul, Parana and Rio de Janeiro. Inclusion criteria: the group exchanged messages about the presidential election, had at least four family members, and the donor had not deleted messages during October 2018. All political multimedia posts from October 2018 were retained (472), and each was verified as completely true, partially false or totally false using the checklist from G1's 'Fato ou Fake' manual. Threats to validity: self-selected convenience sample of ten families, no probability weighting, Android export limits meant some users forwarded posts manually, potential deletion of content before donation, and self-selection on the outcome (22 people declined because they had left their family group over election arguments or wiped its content). No inter-rater reliability, no coder count, no ambiguity-resolution rule reported. The authors name the small family sample (10) as their main limitation while stressing the 190 participants.
